fact.thing: gap between staying invested and switching to a GIC after the 2008 bottom
fact.box: NEI's example: $10,000 balanced portfolio started at the beginning of 2007
fact.claim: In NEI's illustration, $10,000 put into a balanced portfolio at the start of 2007 fell to $7,530 by March 2009, when global stocks hit bottom. Moving what was left into a 5-year GIC grew it to about $10,569 by the end of the chart in 2025, which is roughly the original $10,000. Staying invested grew it to about $34,862, so the gap is about $24,293. NEI calls the chart illustrative. It uses index data, so it leaves out fees and taxes, and it assumes the switch happened at the exact bottom.
sources: NEI INVESTMENTS, BEAR MARKET DECISION FOR THE BALANCED INVESTOR

felt.how: stayed invested vs switched to a GIC at the March 2009 bottom, on $10,000 from 2007, at 2025

sources.label: NEI INVESTMENTS, BEAR MARKET DECISION FOR THE BALANCED INVESTOR
sources.what: If you invested 10,000 in a balanced portfolio at the start of 2007, by March 2009, the month global stocks hit bottom after the financial crisis, your investment was worth $7,530 – a drop of nearly 25%. If you threw in the towel at that point and invested your remaining money in a 5-year GIC (not knowing of course that it was the bottom), 18 years later, you would have earned back your initial capital. If you had simply stayed invested, you would have more than tripled your money.

plain.what: In 2008 the TSX, Canada's main stock market, crashed. In an example from NEI, $10,000 put into a balanced portfolio — a mix of stocks and bonds — at the start of 2007 was worth only $7,530 by March 2009, the bottom. From there, money left in the mix grew to about $34,862 by 2025, while money moved into a 5-year GIC, a bank deposit with a fixed rate, grew to about $10,569, roughly the $10,000 it started with.
plain.so_what: Same $10,000 and the same drop, but the two paths ended about $24,293 apart. NEI calls this an illustration, and it leaves out fees and taxes.
plain.do: Write down, in dollars, how much your own balance dropped the last time it fell.
